system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 10 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with complex bariatric surgical history (prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass with subsequent gastrostomy tube management and later bypass reversal) was admitted for nausea, vomiting, watery diarrhea, and abdominal pain localized to the G-tube site after restarting tube feeds and then developing poor oral tolerance. She was managed supportively with bowel rest, intravenous fluids, antiemetics, resumption of ulcer/GERD prophylaxis (pantoprazole and sucralfate), and close monitoring of intake/output and labs, without evidence of fever, bleeding, or other signs of infection during hospitalization. Pain control was transitioned from IV morphine to oral oxycodone once she tolerated diet; Psychiatry was consulted for anxiety, and a clonidine patch was considered but not continued due to intermittently low systolic blood pressures. By hospital day 2 her diet was advanced to regular and was well tolerated, symptoms improved, and she was discharged home ambulatory and hemodynamically stable with return precautions and continuation of home medications including PRN ondansetron and short-course oxycodone.
problems: Major depressive disorder, single episode, unspecified
Personal history of Methicillin resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I’m Dr. Patel from the medicine team. I understand you came in with abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, and diarrhea. Can you tell me where the pain is worst right now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It started on the right upper side, but now it’s more on the lower right. It’s sharp and it comes in waves.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any blood in the vomit or stool? Any black stools?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No blood. The diarrhea was brown and loose. I’ve been dry heaving more than actually throwing up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any fevers, chills, or anyone at home sick with similar symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fever. No one else is sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. In the ED your vital signs were stable and your bloodwork looked reassuring—no high white count, liver tests similar to your baseline, and your pancreas enzyme was normal. We also did a CT scan and an ultrasound of the right upper abdomen; both didn’t show gallstones, gallbladder infection, or any blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So why does it hurt so much if the scans are normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the frustrating part. With your history—gastric bypass and then reversal—some people get recurrent flares of pain and nausea even when imaging doesn’t show a dangerous cause. We still take it seriously, but right now we don’t see signs of obstruction, perforation, gallbladder disease, or pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be an ulcer again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s less likely because you recently had an upper endoscopy that didn’t show a marginal ulcer and the biopsies were normal. We’ll keep you on your stomach-protecting meds—pantoprazole and sucralfate—and monitor for any bleeding symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: For now, our plan is IV fluids since you’ve had trouble keeping things down, anti-nausea medication, and pain control while we watch how things evolve. We’ll also send stool studies if you’re still having diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I couldn’t even take my morning meds at home. Am I going to miss them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll restart your home meds as soon as you can tolerate them. Some we can give here in the hospital on schedule. We’ll also continue your Keppra for seizures and your psychiatric medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My nausea is still bad. Can I get something stronger?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—let’s use ondansetron as needed, and we’ll keep the IV fluids going. If you’re still vomiting, we can adjust the regimen, but we’ll start with what has worked for you before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Quick check-in: are you still having diarrhea this morning?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a couple times since I got upstairs. No blood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. We’ll collect a stool sample for culture. We also ordered C. diff testing, but it only works if the stool is watery—not formed—so we’ll see what we can send based on what you pass.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m scared this is going to turn into another long admission. I can’t keep doing this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I hear you. Our goal is to make sure there isn’t something dangerous we’re missing, then get your symptoms controlled and get you back home safely. Right now the tests are reassuring, and we’ll take it day by day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How was the night—any vomiting? How’s the pain location today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No vomiting overnight, just nausea. Pain is still mostly lower right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any diarrhea since yesterday afternoon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It slowed down a lot. I haven’t gone since late last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s helpful. Sometimes these episodes start with diarrhea and then swing toward constipation, especially if we use opioid pain meds. We want to be careful because constipation can worsen pain and nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But the pain is real. The IV meds help the most.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I believe you’re in pain. At the same time, IV opioids can make the gut slow down and can trap you in a cycle—more constipation, more pain, more nausea. Since your imaging doesn’t show a surgical problem, we want to shift toward safer options and use oral meds when possible.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So you’re saying no IV pain meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll treat your pain, but we’re going to prioritize non-opioid strategies and avoid escalating IV opioids. You can’t take NSAIDs because of your ulcer history and allergy, and some other pain meds aren’t safe with your current antidepressant regimen. One option we can start is gabapentin, which can help with nerve-related pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gabapentin is for nerves, right? How would that help my stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—sometimes after multiple abdominal surgeries, the nerves and the way the brain processes pain signals can become sensitized. Gabapentin can reduce that nerve signaling. It won’t work instantly, but over days it can help reduce the baseline pain and the flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I tried a nerve block before and it didn’t work. Why would this be different?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: A nerve block targets a specific area; gabapentin works more broadly on nerve signaling. It’s not guaranteed, but it’s one of the better non-opioid options we have given your medication interactions and ulcer history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s your appetite today? Any ability to keep down liquids or food?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can sip and I ate a little. Still nauseous though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s progress. We’ll keep advancing slowly as tolerated. We’ll also keep your pantoprazole and sucralfate on board.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My G-tube site isn’t red, but could the tube be causing this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: On exam the site looks healthy, and the CT showed the gastrostomy tube is appropriately positioned. So it doesn’t look like the tube is displaced or infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a bowel movement now. I feel bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for telling me. Constipation can definitely worsen bloating and nausea. Let’s start a bowel regimen—stool softener and stimulant laxative—and use Miralax as needed. We’ll also encourage walking and fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Won’t laxatives make the pain worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Sometimes you can get cramping as things start moving, but overall relieving the stool burden usually improves pain and nausea. We’ll go stepwise and reassess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How are you feeling on the gabapentin so far—any dizziness or sleepiness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little sleepy, but the pain is maybe slightly less constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good sign. We’ll continue to slowly increase the dose as tolerated, aiming for better pain control without opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s been days. I still haven’t gone. I’m worried something is blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given no bowel movement for several days, it’s reasonable to check. We’re going to get an abdominal X-ray today to look for obstruction versus stool buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your abdominal X-ray is back. It does not show a bowel obstruction. It does show mild fecal loading—basically stool sitting in the colon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s constipation causing all this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a big contributor right now—especially to the nausea and the pressure-type discomfort. The earlier diarrhea resolved quickly, and then the gut slowed down. Opioids can worsen that, which is why we’re trying to avoid them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like you think I’m making it up when I ask for IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry it’s felt that way. I do not think you’re making it up. My job is to treat your pain and also avoid treatments that can prolong the problem or cause harm. With constipation on imaging, IV opioids would likely set you back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any bowel movement overnight after the bowel meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. I’m passing some gas though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Passing gas is a good sign. We’ll continue senna and docusate, and use Miralax as needed. If you still don’t go, we can add a suppository.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They took a stool sample but it wasn’t watery. Does that matter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—C. difficile testing requires a loose, unformed stool. If the sample is formed, the lab cancels it because the result wouldn’t be reliable. We did send stool cultures, and so far they’re negative for common bacteria like Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on your course—diarrhea resolving quickly, stable vitals, and negative cultures—an ongoing bacterial infection is unlikely right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My belly hurts more after the laxatives. It’s like cramping and pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That can happen as the intestines start moving again. Sometimes gas builds up too. We can add simethicone for gas pain, and keep encouraging walking, which helps move gas along.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. I just don’t want to be miserable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The simethicone actually helped. I’m less bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. Let’s keep it as needed. How’s your nausea with eating today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I ate most of lunch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you look more comfortable. How’s the pain compared to admission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s still there, but it’s not as intense. I’ve been walking the halls like you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ve been increasing gabapentin gradually, and the goal is to get you on a stable dose you can continue at home. We’re also keeping acetaminophen scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going home with any opioids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Given the constipation and the lack of a surgical cause on imaging, opioids are more likely to worsen your symptoms. The discharge plan is scheduled acetaminophen, gabapentin, and a bowel regimen to keep things moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if the pain flares again at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have severe worsening pain, persistent vomiting, blood in stool or vomit, black stools, fever, or you can’t keep fluids down, you should come back. For milder flares, use the scheduled meds, keep your bowel regimen, and contact your outpatient team. We also want you to follow up with the chronic pain service to discuss other non-opioid options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They told me my ultrasound showed fatty liver. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound described an echogenic liver consistent with fatty change, which you’ve had noted before. By itself it doesn’t explain this acute pain episode. It’s something to follow with your outpatient doctors—often managed with lifestyle and monitoring labs over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is discharge day if you feel ready. You’ve been tolerating a regular diet, walking independently, and your exam is stable. How are you feeling about going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nervous, but I do feel better than when I came in. I just don’t want to bounce back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Let’s review the plan so you feel prepared: continue pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate for stomach protection; continue your home meds including Keppra, fluoxetine, aripiprazole, and atorvastatin; and new meds are scheduled acetaminophen, gabapentin three times a day, plus senna and docusate twice a day, Miralax as needed, bisacodyl as needed, and simethicone as needed for gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gabapentin is 900 three times a day? That sounds like a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is a higher dose, but we increased it gradually here and you tolerated it. The main side effects are sleepiness and dizziness—so avoid driving if you feel impaired, and let your outpatient team know if it’s too sedating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my nausea meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have ondansetron as needed for nausea. The best prevention is keeping constipation under control and staying hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stool tests—anything I need to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing further right now. The bacterial stool cultures were negative, and the C. diff test was cancelled because the sample was formed. Since your diarrhea resolved, we’re not pursuing more infectious testing unless symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you leave: please schedule follow-up with the chronic pain service. They’ve seen you before and may not recommend opioids, but they can help with non-opioid strategies and adjusting gabapentin. If you develop severe pain with vomiting, fever, bleeding, or inability to eat or drink, come back to the ED.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex bariatric surgical history (prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass with later open reversal and gastrostomy tube in place) was admitted for acute on chronic abdominal pain with nausea/vomiting and diarrhea. Initial evaluation showed stable vital signs and reassuring labs; CT abdomen/pelvis and right upper quadrant ultrasound found no acute intraabdominal process, no biliary obstruction, and an appropriately positioned G-tube, with ultrasound noting fatty liver. Diarrhea resolved early and symptoms evolved into constipation, with abdominal radiograph showing mild fecal loading and no obstruction; stool cultures were negative and C. difficile testing was cancelled due to formed stool. Pain management emphasized non-opioid strategies given ulcer/NSAID intolerance and opioid-associated constipation, including scheduled acetaminophen, gradual uptitration of gabapentin, bowel regimen (senna/docusate with PRN polyethylene glycol and bisacodyl), and PRN simethicone for gas, while continuing home acid suppression and chronic medications. She tolerated a regular diet, ambulated independently, and was discharged home without opioids with outpatient chronic pain follow-up and return precautions.

conversation_lines.text: So it’s constipation causing all this?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a big contributor right now—especially to the nausea and the pressure-type discomfort. The earlier diarrhea resolved quickly, and then the gut slowed down. Opioids can worsen that, which is why we’re trying to avoid them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel like you think I’m making it up when I ask for IV meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m sorry it’s felt that way. I do not think you’re making it up. My job is to treat your pain and also avoid treatments that can prolong the problem or cause harm. With constipation on imaging, IV opioids would likely set you back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Any bowel movement overnight after the bowel meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. I’m passing some gas though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Passing gas is a good sign. We’ll continue senna and docusate, and use Miralax as needed. If you still don’t go, we can add a suppository.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They took a stool sample but it wasn’t watery. Does that matter?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes—C. difficile testing requires a loose, unformed stool. If the sample is formed, the lab cancels it because the result wouldn’t be reliable. We did send stool cultures, and so far they’re negative for common bacteria like Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Based on your course—diarrhea resolving quickly, stable vitals, and negative cultures—an ongoing bacterial infection is unlikely right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My belly hurts more after the laxatives. It’s like cramping and pressure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That can happen as the intestines start moving again. Sometimes gas builds up too. We can add simethicone for gas pain, and keep encouraging walking, which helps move gas along.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. I just don’t want to be miserable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The simethicone actually helped. I’m less bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. Let’s keep it as needed. How’s your nausea with eating today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Better. I ate most of lunch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This morning you look more comfortable. How’s the pain compared to admission?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s still there, but it’s not as intense. I’ve been walking the halls like you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ve been increasing gabapentin gradually, and the goal is to get you on a stable dose you can continue at home. We’re also keeping acetaminophen scheduled.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Am I going home with any opioids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No. Given the constipation and the lack of a surgical cause on imaging, opioids are more likely to worsen your symptoms. The discharge plan is scheduled acetaminophen, gabapentin, and a bowel regimen to keep things moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What if the pain flares again at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you have severe worsening pain, persistent vomiting, blood in stool or vomit, black stools, fever, or you can’t keep fluids down, you should come back. For milder flares, use the scheduled meds, keep your bowel regimen, and contact your outpatient team. We also want you to follow up with the chronic pain service to discuss other non-opioid options.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They told me my ultrasound showed fatty liver. Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ultrasound described an echogenic liver consistent with fatty change, which you’ve had noted before. By itself it doesn’t explain this acute pain episode. It’s something to follow with your outpatient doctors—often managed with lifestyle and monitoring labs over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today is discharge day if you feel ready. You’ve been tolerating a regular diet, walking independently, and your exam is stable. How are you feeling about going home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Nervous, but I do feel better than when I came in. I just don’t want to bounce back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Let’s review the plan so you feel prepared: continue pantoprazole, ranitidine, and sucralfate for stomach protection; continue your home meds including Keppra, fluoxetine, aripiprazole, and atorvastatin; and new meds are scheduled acetaminophen, gabapentin three times a day, plus senna and docusate twice a day, Miralax as needed, bisacodyl as needed, and simethicone as needed for gas.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Gabapentin is 900 three times a day? That sounds like a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is a higher dose, but we increased it gradually here and you tolerated it. The main side effects are sleepiness and dizziness—so avoid driving if you feel impaired, and let your outpatient team know if it’s too sedating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about my nausea meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll have ondansetron as needed for nausea. The best prevention is keeping constipation under control and staying hydrated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stool tests—anything I need to do?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing further right now. The bacterial stool cultures were negative, and the C. diff test was cancelled because the sample was formed. Since your diarrhea resolved, we’re not pursuing more infectious testing unless symptoms return.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Before you leave: please schedule follow-up with the chronic pain service. They’ve seen you before and may not recommend opioids, but they can help with non-opioid strategies and adjusting gabapentin. If you develop severe pain with vomiting, fever, bleeding, or inability to eat or drink, come back to the ED.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex bariatric surgical history (prior Roux-en-Y gastric bypass with later open reversal and gastrostomy tube in place) was admitted for acute on chronic abdominal pain with nausea/vomiting and diarrhea. Initial evaluation showed stable vital signs and reassuring labs; CT abdomen/pelvis and right upper quadrant ultrasound found no acute intraabdominal process, no biliary obstruction, and an appropriately positioned G-tube, with ultrasound noting fatty liver. Diarrhea resolved early and symptoms evolved into constipation, with abdominal radiograph showing mild fecal loading and no obstruction; stool cultures were negative and C. difficile testing was cancelled due to formed stool. Pain management emphasized non-opioid strategies given ulcer/NSAID intolerance and opioid-associated constipation, including scheduled acetaminophen, gradual uptitration of gabapentin, bowel regimen (senna/docusate with PRN polyethylene glycol and bisacodyl), and PRN simethicone for gas, while continuing home acid suppression and chronic medications. She tolerated a regular diet, ambulated independently, and was discharged home without opioids with outpatient chronic pain follow-up and return precautions.
